payload.title: HTTP4-over-WebTransport Protocol Sandbox — Proposal
payload.body: Engineering proposal for an experimental, receiver-driven "HTTP4" transport: a browser JavaScript client and a Go server over WebTransport datagrams, with the receiver pacing delivery via SRPT-scheduled GRANTs (after Stanford's Homa). Recorded as submitted on 2026-09-22. Section 4 refers to client and server code that was not included in the submission.

blocks.text:
## 1. Executive Summary

Modern web transport protocols (HTTP/3, QUIC) remain sender-driven, utilizing congestion windows (CUBIC/BBR) that allocate network capacity based on fair sharing. Under heavy or unbalanced loads, this results in queue bloat and high tail latencies.

This project aims to implement a functional user-space proof-of-concept for HTTP4, an internet-scale adaptation of Stanford's data-center Homa protocol. By utilizing WebTransport, we will invert network control, allowing the receiver to pace data delivery via explicit Grants scheduled by Shortest Remaining Processing Time (SRPT).

## 2. System Architecture Overview

The sandbox relies on a split-stack implementation. The client handles rendering priority, stream tracking, and grant issuance. The server serves as a compliant, passive data repository that releases bytes only upon structural validation of receiver-driven tokens.

```
┌──────────────────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────────────────┐
│    Web Browser (JS Client)   │              │     Go Backend Server        │
│                              │              │                              │
│  ┌────────────────────────┐  │              │  ┌────────────────────────┐  │
│  │   UI Rendering Stack   │  │              │  │  Static Resource Pool  │  │
│  └───────────┬────────────┘  │              │  └───────────▲────────────┘  │
│              │ (Priority)    │              │              │ (Byte Slices) │
│  ┌───────────▼────────────┐  │ WebTransport │  ┌───────────┴────────────┐  │
│  │  SRPT Grant Scheduler  ├──┼─► Datagrams ─┼─►│ Passive Sender Engine  │  │
│  └────────────────────────┘  │  (UDP 443)   │  └────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────┘              └──────────────────────────────┘
```

### Protocol Interaction Lifecycle

1. **Unscheduled Initiation:** The client sends an un-granted, unscheduled Datagram requesting an asset ID.
2. **Metadata Priming:** The server replies with Packet 0 containing the total payload dimensions.
3. **Paced Evaluation:** The client inserts the transaction into its local SRPT map, calculates weight modifications (based on asset type or viewport visibility), and emits GRANT datagrams.
4. **Passive Emission:** The server pushes packet offsets exactly matching the granted ceiling.

## 3. Wire Format Specification (HTTP4 Datagram Frame)

To maximize throughput, all control and data packets are encapsulated directly into WebTransport Datagrams (restricted to an MTU boundary of 1200 bytes).

### Plaintext Common Header (All Packets)

- Byte 0: Packet Type (0x01: REQ, 0x02: DATA, 0x03: GRANT, 0x04: RESEND)
- Bytes 1-8: RPC_ID (64-bit cryptographic identifier matching Request/Response pairs)

### Payload Layouts (Post-Header Encapsulation)

**0x02: DATA (Server ➔ Client)**

| Total Size (4 Bytes) | Chunk Offset (4 Bytes) | Encrypted Byte Stream |
|---|---|---|

**0x03: GRANT (Client ➔ Server)**

| Max Offset (4 Bytes) | Priority Class (1B) |
|---|---|

**0x04: RESEND (Client ➔ Server)**

| Missing Start (4 Bytes) | Missing End (4 Bytes) |
|---|---|

## 4. Engineering Implementation Blueprints

Here is the initial software architecture drafted for the sandbox engine.

**Client Implementation (Browser JavaScript):** This script initializes the WebTransport connection, processes raw packet frames, evaluates remaining processing time, and handles rendering priority hooks.

**Server Implementation (Go Engine):** This backend infrastructure runs concurrently using Goroutines, monitoring consumer-driven GRANT updates without generating blocking buffer overhead.

_(The code referred to here was not included in the submitted proposal.)_

## 5. Project Roadmap & Success Benchmarks

```
┌────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────┐
│ Phase 1: Local Loop    │ ───► │ Phase 2: WAN Injection │ ───► │ Phase 3: Starvation Fix│
│ Datagram verification  │      │ Apply artificial loss  │      │ Age weight adjustments │
└────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────┘
```

To evaluate the validity of this architecture against native HTTP/3, testing will be executed across three evaluation goals:

- **Success Metric 1 (Tail Latency Minimization):** Under asymmetric multi-asset transfers, the 99th percentile recovery time for tool-calling API frames must experience an 80%+ decline relative to multiplexed HTTP/3 streams.
- **Success Metric 2 (Head-of-Line Elimination):** Heavy background image loads must not stall or produce structural delays on parallel layout-blocking styles.
- **Success Metric 3 (Pacing Transparency):** Verify through network capture software that the server emits zero un-granted bursts, confirming absolute client-side control over network pipelines.

payload.title: G1 — Local loop delivers every asset intact over the HTTP4 datagram protocol
payload.body: Phase 1 correctness. A fixed set of assets (1 KB – 50 MB) requested via REQ → Packet 0 → GRANT → DATA (+ RESEND) on a local WebTransport session must reassemble byte-for-byte. Measured as % of assets in the integrity suite whose SHA-256 matches the source.

payload.title: G2 — Server emits zero un-granted bytes (pacing transparency)
payload.body: Proposal Success Metric 3. The server must never send DATA past the highest granted offset for an RPC (beyond the agreed unscheduled Packet 0). Measured server-side: a counter of bytes sent beyond the grant ceiling, summed over a test run. A packet capture cannot show this because QUIC encrypts every datagram; use server counters or qlog.

payload.title: G3 — p99 latency of small API responses under mixed load drops ≥80% vs HTTP/3
payload.body: Proposal Success Metric 1. Workload: small (≤4 KB) API-style responses competing with large asset transfers. Metric: % reduction in p99 completion time for the small responses, HTTP4 vs multiplexed HTTP/3 streams, same hosts and network conditions. Note: WebTransport datagrams remain subject to QUIC's own congestion control, so this measures receiver-side SRPT scheduling on top of QUIC, not a replacement for it.

payload.title: G4 — Heavy image loads do not delay layout-blocking styles
payload.body: Proposal Success Metric 2. Metric: % increase in stylesheet completion time when a large background image transfer runs in parallel, vs the same stylesheet loaded alone. Target not yet set — see the open question on the allowed slowdown.

payload.title: G5 — Correctness and pacing hold under WAN loss and delay
payload.body: Phase 2. Metric: % of cells in the impairment matrix (loss 0/1/5% × RTT 0/50/150 ms) where G1 and G2 both hold.

payload.title: G6 — Large transfers are never starved by SRPT
payload.body: Phase 3. Under a sustained stream of small requests, the worst-case slowdown of a large transfer (completion time ÷ its completion time with no competition). Target not yet set — see the open question on the starvation bound.

payload.title: What slowdown of stylesheet loads is acceptable while a large image downloads (G4 target)?
payload.body: The proposal says heavy image loads 'must not stall or produce structural delays' on layout-blocking styles, but gives no number. G4 measures the % increase in stylesheet completion time with a parallel large image vs alone. With QUIC congestion control still underneath, 0% is not physically achievable; some contention is unavoidable.

options.consequence: Strict; demonstrates near-complete isolation. Likely needs priority classes to preempt the image aggressively.
Moderate; clearly better than typical HTTP/3 contention while leaving room for QUIC-level effects.

options.option: Relative: ≥X% better than the HTTP/3 baseline
options.consequence: Measures improvement rather than an absolute bound; requires the HTTP/3 baseline harness before G4 can be scored.

payload.title: What worst-case slowdown for large transfers counts as 'not starved' (G6 target)?
payload.body: Pure SRPT can starve a large transfer indefinitely while small requests keep arriving. Phase 3 adds age-based weight adjustments. G6 needs a bound on completion time ÷ uncontended completion time for a large transfer under sustained small-request load.

options.consequence: Tight fairness; aging must kick in early, which erodes some of G3's tail-latency win.
Balanced; small requests keep strong priority but large ones are guaranteed to finish.
Favours G3 heavily; only prevents true starvation.

payload.title: Phase 1: Local loop — datagram protocol working end to end on localhost
payload.body: Parent for Phase 1 of the HTTP4 sandbox (doc-sjj28a2). Done when the integrity suite scores G1 = 100% and G2 = 0 un-granted bytes on a localhost WebTransport session.

payload.title: Scaffold repo: Go server module, static JS client, and localhost WebTransport TLS setup
payload.body:
Create `server/` (Go module using quic-go + webtransport-go) and `client/` (plain ES modules served statically). Generate a dev certificate that Chrome accepts for WebTransport on localhost: either a self-signed ECDSA P-256 cert valid ≤14 days passed via `serverCertificateHashes`, or a locally trusted CA (mkcert). Add a script that regenerates the cert and prints its SHA-256 hash for the client.

Acceptance: the browser opens a WebTransport session to the Go server on localhost and one echo datagram goes each way.

payload.title: Specify and implement the HTTP4 datagram codec in Go and JS with shared test vectors
payload.body:
Implement encode/decode for REQ, DATA, GRANT, and RESEND per doc-sjj28a2 §3 (1-byte type + 8-byte RPC_ID header; big-endian fields). Write a spec at `docs/wire-format.md` that fills the gaps the proposal leaves:
- **REQ payload** is not defined: specify how the asset ID is encoded (e.g. a 2-byte length plus UTF-8 path).
- **Packet 0**: define it as a DATA packet at offset 0 carrying Total Size and the first unscheduled bytes, and fix how many unscheduled bytes the server may send before any GRANT. G2 depends on this number.
- **RPC_ID**: the client generates it as 8 random bytes via `crypto.getRandomValues`.
- **Payload sizing**: data per packet = `maxDatagramSize` − 17. Use the negotiated size, never a hard-coded 1200.
- **Encryption**: drop the extra "Encrypted Byte Stream" layer, because QUIC already encrypts datagrams, and record that as a decision.

Acceptance: golden hex vectors in `testdata/wire/` round-trip identically through both the Go and JS codecs, including a malformed/truncated input set that must be rejected.

payload.title: Build the asset fixture set for the integrity suite
payload.body:
Create a deterministic set of test assets for the server's static resource pool: 1 KB, 4 KB, 64 KB, 1 MB, 10 MB, and 50 MB, plus edge sizes (0 bytes, exactly one payload, one payload + 1 byte). Generate them from a seeded PRNG rather than checking large files in, and emit a manifest of SHA-256 hashes.

Acceptance: `scripts/gen-fixtures` reproduces identical files and manifest on every run.

payload.title: Server passive sender: answer REQ with Packet 0 and send DATA only up to the granted offset
payload.body:
In the Go server, keep per-RPC state (asset, total size, grant ceiling, next offset) keyed by RPC_ID. On REQ: look up the asset, send Packet 0 plus at most the unscheduled allowance from the wire spec. On GRANT: raise the ceiling (ignore any grant that lowers it) and send DATA up to it. Use one goroutine per session, and never block the datagram receive loop on sending.

Instrument for G2: count bytes per RPC sent past ceiling + unscheduled allowance, and expose the totals (metrics endpoint or JSON on shutdown). The counter must be checked at the send path itself, not inferred afterwards.

Acceptance: unit tests with a fake transport show zero sends past the ceiling for grants that arrive out of order, repeat, or are missing. Unknown asset IDs and unknown RPC_IDs are handled without panicking.

payload.title: JS client: request assets, reassemble DATA, and issue grants from a basic SRPT scheduler
payload.body:
In the browser client: open the session, read `transport.datagrams.maxDatagramSize`, and send REQ. On Packet 0, add the RPC to an SRPT map keyed by remaining bytes. Keep a fixed grant window (e.g. a set number of bytes in flight) and give it to the RPC with the fewest remaining bytes first. Reassemble into a preallocated buffer and track which byte ranges have arrived. Resolve a promise with the bytes when complete.

Phase 1 uses size only for scheduling. Priority classes and viewport weighting come later, but GRANT should already carry the priority byte.

Acceptance: fetching a single asset and several concurrent assets both return correct bytes on a lossless localhost link, and an instrumented run shows the smallest remaining RPC is always granted first.

payload.title: Recover lost datagrams with RESEND: client gap detection and server retransmit
payload.body:
Datagrams are unreliable even on localhost, because they are dropped when buffers fill. Client: when bytes below the grant ceiling haven't arrived within a timeout (based on the measured RTT, with a floor), send RESEND for each missing range, with backoff and a retry limit. Server: on RESEND, resend exactly the missing range, capped at the grant ceiling. A resend of granted bytes is not an un-granted byte, and the G2 counter must not count it.

Also handle a lost REQ or Packet 0: the client resends REQ with the same RPC_ID if Packet 0 doesn't arrive in time, and the server answers repeat REQs without creating a second RPC.

Acceptance: with a test hook that drops a chosen set of datagrams (every Nth, a Packet 0, the final chunk), every transfer still completes with the correct hash.

payload.title: Automated Phase 1 integrity suite in headless Chrome that reports G1 and G2
payload.body:
Write a script (Playwright + headless Chromium) that starts the Go server with the fixture pool and loads the client. It fetches every fixture one at a time and then all at once, and compares SHA-256 hashes against the manifest. At the end it reads the server's un-granted byte counter and prints both figures as JSON: `{ "g1_pct_intact": …, "g2_ungranted_bytes": … }`. Run it once with no drops and once with the RESEND drop hook enabled.

Acceptance: one command runs the whole suite with a non-zero exit on failure. Its output is the evidence for recording measurements against G1 and G2 and closing Phase 1.

payload.title: Project layout: server/ (Go module) + client/ (browser) with shared testdata/, docs/, scripts/, tests/ at root
payload.body: Chosen by the user while scaffolding iss-ajda0b4. The Go module lives in server/ with cmd/http4d and internal/. The browser client lives in client/. Wire vectors, assets, and the spec are shared at the repo root, and a root package.json holds dev dependencies only. This matches the `touches` paths already recorded on the Phase 1 issues. Rejected: B, Go module at repo root with web/ (more idiomatic `go test ./...`, but the issue paths would need changing); C, spec/ plus impl/go and impl/js (more structure than a two-implementation sandbox needs).

payload.title: Dev TLS: server generates an in-memory self-signed ECDSA cert at startup and serves its SHA-256 for serverCertificateHashes
payload.body: Chosen by the user while scaffolding iss-ajda0b4. At each start the server creates a P-256 cert valid for less than 14 days, as serverCertificateHashes requires, and exposes the hash on the same origin that serves the page. With no files on disk and no manual renewal, expiry never breaks local runs. This replaces the 'regenerate cert script' named in the issue. Rejected: cert files plus a scripts/devcert regenerator (has to be re-run every 14 days or fewer); mkcert (not installed, and it modifies the system trust store).

payload.title: Client is written in TypeScript and bundled with a one-shot esbuild build to client/dist
payload.body: Chosen by the user while scaffolding iss-ajda0b4. Full TypeScript, with tsc --noEmit for type checking and esbuild for bundling. There is no watch mode or dev server; the user's standing rule is 'never run dev task'. Rejected: JS with JSDoc and tsc --checkJs (no build step, but weaker types); plain JS.

payload.title: Browser acceptance checks run as one-shot headless tests that start the server, drive Chromium, and exit
payload.body: Chosen by the user while scaffolding iss-ajda0b4. The user's standing rule is 'never run dev task', so agents never leave a long-lived dev server running. Browser verification is a one-shot test process that owns the server's whole lifecycle. Rejected: the user runs the server by hand; a Go-only WebTransport client check with the browser deferred.

payload.title: Chrome 153 reports WebTransport maxDatagramSize = 1024 bytes on a localhost session, below the proposal's 1200-byte assumption
payload.body: Measured by the scaffold echo test: Google Chrome 153.0.8010.53, headless, macOS arm64, against the quic-go v0.63 / webtransport-go v0.13 server on 127.0.0.1, with `transport.datagrams.maxDatagramSize` read after `ready`. Result 1024. With the 17-byte DATA header (9 common + 8), that leaves at most 1007 payload bytes per datagram, not ~1183. This is one browser and version on loopback; other paths and browsers may report different values, so codec sizing must use the negotiated value at runtime.

payload.title: Headless Chrome loads the client from the Go server, opens a WebTransport session trusted only via serverCertificateHashes, sends one datagram, and receives the identical datagram back. The test starts and stops the server itself, and no process is left running.

payload.evidence: `npm run test:echo` on 2026-09-22 (Chrome 153.0.8010.53, Go 1.27.1, Node 24.14.1) → ✔ 1/1, echo {"ok":true,"attempts":1,"rttMs":1,"maxDatagramSize":1024}; `pgrep http4d` found no process afterwards. To re-check: `npm install && npm test`.

payload.title: Go server tests pass: dev cert is ECDSA, valid for under 14 days, and its hash matches the DER; a Go WebTransport client with a hash-pinned cert gets the datagram echoed; a foreign Origin gets 403; the loopback origin rules hold.

payload.evidence: `cd server && go vet ./... && go test -count=1 ./...` on 2026-09-22 → ok internal/devcert, ok internal/server.

payload.title: Unscheduled bytes are client-authorized: REQ carries initial_grant, and the server treats it as a GRANT for [0, initial_grant)
payload.body:
Resolves the 'Packet 0 / unscheduled allowance' gap named in iss-2atv8th. Homa lets a sender push a fixed amount of unscheduled data (about one RTT's worth) before any grant. Here the client names that amount itself in a u32 field on REQ. The server never sends a byte the client did not authorize, so G2 is a strict zero with no exemption for a first burst, and the client can still ask for Homa-style unscheduled bytes by setting initial_grant to about one BDP. Packet 0 is always the DATA packet at offset 0 and is sent even when initial_grant = 0, with an empty payload that only delivers total_size.

Rejected: a server-side constant allowance U. It creates a G2 exemption that the server has to account for, and the receiver cannot tune it per request (e.g. 0 for below-the-fold images).

payload.title: Add ERROR packet type 0x05 (NOT_FOUND, BAD_REQUEST, UNKNOWN_RPC) to the wire format
payload.body: The proposal defines no failure signal. Without one, a REQ for an unknown asset, or a GRANT or RESEND for an RPC the server has forgotten, gets no answer, and the client can only time out. ERROR is 10 bytes (header plus a 1-byte code) and ends the RPC. Decoders accept unknown codes so that codes can be added later without breaking older decoders. Rejected: silently dropping such packets (the client can't tell loss from failure, which inflates tail latency); overloading DATA with a sentinel total_size (ambiguous for empty assets).

payload.title: No application-layer encryption: the DATA payload is plaintext asset bytes inside QUIC's encryption
payload.body: The proposal's DATA layout says 'Encrypted Byte Stream' and its header 'Plaintext'. Every WebTransport datagram is already encrypted and authenticated by QUIC (TLS 1.3), so a second layer adds CPU cost and key management and protects nothing more. The rpc_id is random for collision avoidance, not secrecy. Rejected: per-RPC AEAD over the payload.

payload.title: All 10 hand-written valid vectors in testdata/wire/vectors.json decode to the expected packet and re-encode to identical hex, in both the Go and TS codecs; all 20 invalid vectors are rejected by both.

payload.evidence: `npm test` on 2026-09-22: `ok http4/server/internal/wire` (TestVectorsValid, TestVectorsInvalid), `node --test tests/wire/wire.test.ts` 35/35 pass. To re-check: `npm run test:go && npm run test:wire`.

payload.title: Decoding never panics or throws anything but a malformed-packet error, and every accepted input re-encodes byte-for-byte, so each packet has exactly one encoding.

payload.evidence: Go: `cd server && go test -run='^$' -fuzz=FuzzDecode -fuzztime=30s ./internal/wire/` → 7,577,245 execs, PASS. TS: randomized test in tests/wire/wire.test.ts, 200k seeded inputs (mutated vectors + random buffers), pass.

payload.title: With a fake transport whose send path checks every DATA against the highest grant the test client sent, the server sends zero bytes past the grant when grants arrive out of order, repeated, lowered, past the end, or missing (initial_grant 0), including a seeded randomized run over 12 RPCs with REQ repeats, RESENDs, and a mid-run chunk-size cut. The server's own UngrantedSent counter is also 0.

payload.evidence: `cd server && go test -race -count=20 ./internal/sender/` on 2026-09-22 → ok (20/20). Tests: TestGrantsAreCumulativeAndMonotone, TestZeroInitialGrantSendsOnlySize, TestRandomizedGrantDiscipline, etc. in server/internal/sender/sender_test.go.

payload.title: Unknown asset → ERROR NOT_FOUND; GRANT/RESEND for an unknown or evicted RPC → ERROR UNKNOWN_RPC; malformed packets and client-sent DATA are dropped and the session keeps working; no panics.

payload.evidence: TestErrors, TestMalformedAndClientOnlyPacketsAreDropped, TestIdleRPCsAreEvicted in server/internal/sender/sender_test.go; `go test -race ./internal/sender/` passes.

payload.title: The receive loop keeps processing GRANTs while every send is blocked (QUIC queue full), and a real-QUIC HTTP4 fetch of a 300,000-byte asset with a windowed client reassembles exactly, with /metrics.json reporting ungranted_bytes_sent = 0.

payload.evidence: TestReceiveNotBlockedBySend (sender); TestHTTP4FetchOverQUIC and TestMetricsEndpoint (server) on 2026-09-22 → metrics {DataPackets:257 DataBytes:300000 ResentBytes:0 ChunkShrinks:0 UngrantedSent:0}. Re-check: `cd server && go test -race -run 'HTTP4|Metrics' -v ./internal/server/`. The full `npm test` (typecheck, Go, TS wire, Chrome echo) also passes.

patch.body:
Datagrams are unreliable even on localhost, because they are dropped when buffers fill. Client: when bytes below the grant ceiling haven't arrived within a timeout (based on the measured RTT, with a floor), send RESEND for each missing range, with backoff and a retry limit. Server: on RESEND, resend exactly the missing range, capped at the grant ceiling. A resend of granted bytes is not an un-granted byte, and the G2 counter must not count it.

Also handle a lost REQ or Packet 0: the client resends REQ with the same RPC_ID if Packet 0 doesn't arrive in time, and the server answers repeat REQs without creating a second RPC.

Acceptance: with a test hook that drops a chosen set of datagrams (every Nth, a Packet 0, the final chunk), every transfer still completes with the correct hash.

Update 2026-09-22 (from iss-7fp0jtf): the server half already exists in server/internal/sender. RESEND is clipped to [start, min(end, granted, sent)); repeated REQs resend Packet 0 without creating a new RPC; resent bytes are counted in ResentBytes, never UngrantedSent. The remaining work is the client side (gap detection, timers, backoff) plus a drop-injection hook and the end-to-end acceptance test.
